subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 17 periods = 680 minutes
Total: 17 periods · 11h 20min

periods.activity_title: Navya's Walk Home: Spotting the Postbox
periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Students discuss how the post office helps people stay connected (p. 19)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Navya and grandfather passing the postbox

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to share a time they sent or received something in the mail — a letter, a parcel, a greeting card — and draws out what they know about how it got from one place to another. Students share briefly in pairs before a few pairs report to the class.

Students open Textbook p. 19 and read the section describing Navya's walk past the postbox and her conversation with grandfather about how a posted letter travels. Teacher prompts: What does the postman do after collecting letters? Where do letters go before they reach the right house? Students note two or three steps of the postal journey in their notebooks.

Class discussion: How does the post office help people who live far apart stay in touch? Teacher guides students to articulate the idea that the post office is a shared community service — not just for one family but for everyone in the neighbourhood. The teacher invites students to think about elderly family members or neighbours who may rely on it.

Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks answering the question from Textbook p. 19: 'How does the post office help people stay connected with each other?' Teacher circulates and asks one or two students to share their response aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how a local community institution serves people by connecting them across distance.
periods.section_context: Navya's walk home, postbox, letter collection by postman, post office sorting, postal delivery system.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can you think of anyone in your neighbourhood who might not have a mobile phone — how might they send important news to a relative far away?' This surfaces the continued relevance of the post office without naming any moment to follow.

periods.activity_title: From Drumbeats to Smartphones: A Communication Timeline
periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Students trace the evolution of communication methods across time (p. 21)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of communication methods across history

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the passage from Textbook p. 21 describing how people communicated long ago — drumbeats, rock carvings, messengers, pigeons — moving forward through postal service, telephone, radio, television, and mobile internet. Students listen and, as the teacher pauses, call out each method they hear.

Each student draws a simple timeline strip on their paper or notebook page, labelling at least five communication methods in order from oldest to newest. Beside each, they draw a small picture or symbol. Students who finish early add a word describing how fast or slow that method was.

Students share their timelines with a partner and compare which methods they each included. Teacher facilitates a brief whole-class check: Did everyone have the same starting point? Were there methods some students placed in a different order? Discussion lands on the idea that communication has become faster and more immediate over time.

Students write one sentence at the bottom of their timeline: 'The biggest change in communication has been _____ because _____.' Teacher invites two or three different completions to be read aloud, celebrating varied reasoning.

periods.implied_lo: Students can sequence a set of human-made systems in order of historical development and identify the direction of change.
periods.section_context: Drumbeats, rock carvings, messengers, pigeons, postal service, telephone, radio, television, mobile phones, internet.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to think about what their grandparents say they used — this connects lived family memory to the textbook's historical arc without requiring a formal elder-interview to have taken place beforehand.

periods.activity_title: Slow Letters, Fast Messages: Comparing Then and Now
periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Students discuss with elders how they communicated and compare it with today's methods (p. 20)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the structured comparison task from Textbook p. 20: students will think about how elders in their homes communicated when they were children — the methods they used, how long it took, and what it felt like to wait for news — and contrast this with how students themselves communicate today.

Students work in pairs to brainstorm and fill a two-column table in their notebooks: one column for 'How elders communicated' (drawing on family conversations and the textbook's historical content) and one for 'How we communicate today'. They aim for at least three rows. Teacher circulates, prompting: Was it faster or slower? Could it reach everywhere? How did people feel when a message was delayed?

Pairs share one contrast with the class. Teacher builds a shared table on the board from student contributions. Discussion from Textbook p. 21 prompts: How did the slow pace of letters affect people's lives in the past? What has changed now that messages are instant?

Students individually write two or three sentences in response to the discussion prompt from Textbook p. 21: 'Today quick messages make sharing the news easier, but sometimes wrong information spreads very quickly too. How can we ensure the news we share is true?' Teacher collects or reviews notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare communication practices across generations and draw a reasoned conclusion about how changes in speed affect everyday life.
periods.section_context: Slow letters, waiting for news, elder communication practices, instant digital messages, misinformation spread, checking news accuracy.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'If you sent a letter to a friend in another city and it took three weeks to arrive, what kinds of news would have changed by then?' This makes the speed contrast concrete and personal.

periods.textbook_anchor: On Our Way Back Home — Students write a letter to a friend and post it (p. 18)
materials: Envelope (one per student or one shared demonstration envelope)
periods.visual_aids: Teacher-drawn or textbook diagram showing the parts of a letter and an addressed envelope

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 18 and walks students through the activity: writing a letter to a friend. On the board, the teacher draws and labels the three key parts — sender's address, body of the letter, recipient's address on the envelope. Students identify what information goes in each part.

Students compose a short letter on their writing paper or notebook page to a real or imagined friend, sharing one piece of news or asking one question. They then write out the recipient's address and their own return address on a separate slip (simulating an envelope). Teacher circulates, supporting spacing and address format.

Students pair up and read each other's letters, checking that the greeting, body, and sign-off are present. Partners suggest one small improvement. Teacher then demonstrates how a stamp is placed and how the envelope is sealed, connecting back to the postal journey discussed earlier.

Class reflects briefly: What did it feel like to write by hand compared to sending a quick message? Teacher draws out the idea that a written letter carries care and effort — a value many families still associate with handwritten communication.

periods.implied_lo: Students can produce a structured written communication that follows a conventional format.
periods.section_context: Handwritten letter format, sender's address, recipient's address, envelope, stamp, postal delivery.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite students to think about whether anyone in their family still writes or keeps handwritten letters — grandparents, relatives abroad — to surface the continuing personal value of this practice.

periods.activity_title: Banks Then and Now: Keeping Money Safe
periods.textbook_anchor: Savings for the Future — Students discuss which method they would choose to send money and why (p. 25)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of bank, ATM, and passbook

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 25 and reads the passage where Navya and grandfather stop at the bank with the ATM. Discussion opener: What is a bank for? Have you ever been inside a bank with a family member? What did you see? Students share briefly; teacher notes key ideas on the board (safe keeping, savings, withdrawals).

Teacher presents the contrast between past and present banking: long queues, passbooks, money orders through the post office versus today's mobile transfers and UPI. Students open Textbook p. 25 and respond to the three Write prompts — whether they save, where they keep savings, and why saving matters — in their notebooks.

Class discussion from Textbook p. 25: If you had to send money to someone far away, which method would you choose — phone transfer, money order, or another way — and why? Teacher facilitates students comparing the reliability, speed, and accessibility of each method, including for family members without smartphones.

Students write one sentence naming one advantage of a bank over keeping money at home, and one sentence naming one advantage of mobile payment over a money order. Teacher invites two or three students to share, acknowledging that different families may use different methods.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare past and present methods of managing money and explain the role of a community financial institution.
periods.section_context: Bank, ATM, passbook, savings, money order, UPI, mobile payment, long queues, safe keeping.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did any elder in your family ever send or receive a money order? What was it like to wait for the money to arrive?' This surfaces the lived intergenerational contrast without requiring a prior homework task.

periods.activity_title: Reading a Currency Note: Symbols, Languages, and Value
periods.textbook_anchor: Savings for the Future — Students examine an Indian currency note and answer questions about its value, languages, and symbols (p. 26)
materials: One Indian currency note per pair (any denomination, brought by teacher or students)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration or printed image of an Indian currency note (front and back)

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes currency notes (or asks pairs to pool one note between them) and directs students to Textbook p. 26. Teacher sets the observation task: students will look closely at the note and record what they find before reading any answers.

Students observe their note carefully and answer the three questions from Textbook p. 26 in their notebooks: (a) What is the value of the note? (b) How many languages appear on the note? (c) What pictures or symbols are printed on it? Students work in pairs, taking turns pointing out features.

Pairs share findings with the class. Teacher builds a class record on the board: tallying how many languages different pairs counted, listing the symbols named, and noting the denomination values seen. Teacher highlights that Indian currency carries the nation's linguistic diversity and symbols of heritage.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one fact they noticed about the note that surprised them, and one sentence explaining why a currency note needs to show its value clearly. Teacher closes by asking: What does it mean that a note is accepted anywhere in India?

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured close observation of a familiar object and record specific details in an organised way.
periods.section_context: Indian currency note, denomination, languages printed on note, symbols and pictures on note, national symbols.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to count the language panel carefully — many students assume there are only one or two languages. Ask: 'Why do you think so many languages appear on the same note?'

periods.activity_title: How a Bank Works: Roles, Services, and the ATM
periods.textbook_anchor: Savings for the Future — Students find out how a bank works and answer questions about ATMs and other services (p. 26)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook diagram or illustration of a bank interior and ATM

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the inquiry: today students will pool what they know and have observed about banks — from family visits, from the textbook, and from their neighbourhood — to answer two specific questions from Textbook p. 26. Teacher reads both questions aloud: (a) Other than saving money, what else do people use banks for? (b) What is an ATM and how does it help people?

Students work in small groups to brainstorm and discuss both questions, drawing on the textbook passage and their own experience. Each group records their answers in note form. Teacher circulates, prompting: Have you seen what happens at the counter? Have you watched someone use an ATM? What did you notice?

Groups share their answers. Teacher organises responses under two headings on the board: 'Services banks offer' and 'What the ATM does'. Students add any points they missed to their own notebooks. Teacher introduces the passbook as a record-keeping tool, describing its key elements.

Students write a short paragraph (three to four sentences) explaining what an ATM is and how it helps someone who needs cash outside banking hours. Teacher invites one or two students to read their paragraph, correcting any factual gaps gently.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the range of services provided by a local financial institution and explain the function of one specific technological tool within it.
periods.section_context: Bank services, savings, loans, ATM function, passbook, round-the-clock cash access.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'If there were no ATM, what would you have to do to get cash at night or on a holiday?' This makes the ATM's purpose concrete and situationally clear.

periods.activity_title: My Budget Plan: Spending and Saving ₹100
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students plan how to spend and save ₹100 wisely over a month (p. 31)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 31 and introduces the budget task: each student has an imaginary ₹100 for the month and must plan how to spend and save it. Teacher models one example row on the board — for example, ₹10 for stationery — and asks: What else might you spend on? What might you save for?

Students draw a simple budget table in their notebooks with three columns — Item, Amount Spent, Reason — and fill in their spending plan. At the bottom, they calculate how much is left to save and write one sentence about what they are saving toward. Teacher circulates and asks individual students to justify a spending choice.
Small-group share: each student tells their group one thing they decided to save for and one thing they cut back on to save more. Groups briefly discuss: Is it easy to save? What makes it harder?

Whole-class reflection: Teacher asks — 'What is one habit that could help you save a little more each week?' Students share one habit each. Teacher connects this to the chapter's theme: communities and families that save are better prepared for the future.

periods.implied_lo: Students can create a simple plan that balances spending and saving and explain the reasoning behind financial choices.
periods.section_context: ₹100 budget, spending categories (stationery, snacks, toys), savings plan, piggy bank, future needs.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Has anyone at home — a grandparent or parent — told you about something they saved up for over a long time? What was it?' This grounds the saving habit in family and community practice.

periods.activity_title: Public Places in Our Neighbourhood: Who Is There and What Do They Do?
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students list people who work at a hospital or health centre and describe their roles (p. 23)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of neighbourhood public places (hospital, fire station, police station, library)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: What places near your home or school do you think of as 'public places'? Students name what they know; teacher lists responses on the board. Teacher then opens Textbook p. 23 and introduces the section's concept: public places are community infrastructure — they serve health, safety, and everyday life for everyone.

Students open Textbook p. 23 and work on the Write task: listing people who work at a hospital or health centre and describing their role. Students fill the table in their notebooks, starting with the example given and adding at least three more roles (nurse, ambulance driver, pharmacist, ward attendant, health visitor). Teacher circulates and prompts: Has anyone been to a hospital — who did you see working there?

Class shares their hospital-worker tables. Teacher then broadens the discussion: other than hospitals, which public places are in our neighbourhood? What do the people working there do? Students add a few rows for workers at a police station, library, or post office. Teacher highlights community health workers and health camps as a way the health system reaches people who cannot travel.

Students write two sentences: 'A public place I use is ___. The people who work there help the community by ___.' Teacher invites three or four different public places to be shared, ensuring the class sees the breadth of community infrastructure.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify people who work in local public institutions and explain how their roles serve the wider community.
periods.section_context: Hospital, health centre, doctors, nurses, ambulance driver, pharmacist, health visitors, health camps, police station, library, fire station, post office.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which of these public places has someone in your family used recently — and who helped them there?' This connects the abstract idea of community service to personal experience.

periods.activity_title: Transport Then and Now: How We Get Around
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students find out how parents and grandparents travelled when young and compare it to today (p. 23)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of metro, flyover, and traditional transport modes

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 22 and reads the passage about transportation infrastructure — metro trains and flyovers — and the observation that building them sometimes required cutting trees, disrupting birds and animals. Teacher asks: What transport do you use most? Have you noticed any new construction in your area? What was there before?

Students work on the Find out task from Textbook p. 23 in their notebooks: they write what they know (from conversations with parents or grandparents) about how their elders travelled to school or other places when young, and compare this with how they travel today. They write at least two differences. Teacher circulates and prompts: Was it faster or slower? Did they walk more? Did roads or trains exist?

Pairs share their comparisons. Teacher builds a class chart on the board: 'Past modes' versus 'Present modes'. Discussion: Have new transport systems made life easier? What have we gained? What has been lost (trees, open land, animals' habitats)? Teacher surfaces the chapter's environmental trade-off — connectivity versus ecological cost — and Dada ji's suggestion of balancing by planting trees.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one describing a change in transport that has made their neighbourhood more connected, and one describing something that was lost or changed as a result. Teacher invites two contrasting responses to be read aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare past and present transportation practices, identifying both the benefits of new infrastructure and its environmental consequences.
periods.section_context: Metro trains, flyovers, traditional travel modes, trees removed for construction, connectivity, environmental trade-off, tree planting.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If your grandfather walked to school every day, what did he see on the way that you might not see now? Why?' This opens the ecological thread without foreclosing the transport-improvement narrative.

periods.activity_title: Cardinal Directions: Reading Navya's Neighbourhood Map
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students look at the picture and write the places located in the North, East, West, and South of Navya's home (p. 28)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map illustration of Navya's neighbourhood (p. 28)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces cardinal directions by asking students to face toward the classroom's main windows or door and identify which direction they are facing. Teacher draws a compass rose (N, S, E, W) on the board and explains the convention: North is always at the top of a map. Students copy the compass rose into their notebooks.

Students open Textbook p. 28 and look carefully at the picture of Navya's neighbourhood. They complete the Write task: listing the places located to the North, East, West, and South of Navya's home, filling in the table in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, checking that students are correctly reading the compass rose on the textbook map before naming locations.

Class checks answers together. Teacher points to each direction on the board's compass rose while students call out what they found in that direction on Navya's map. Teacher corrects any direction confusion gently — common errors are mixing East and West — and re-explains the compass rose convention.

Students practise applying directions to their own classroom: teacher asks them to name one object or window in each of the four directions. Students record their classroom compass in their notebooks as a simple two-column table (Direction — What I see). This anchors the abstract convention in an immediately observable space.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use cardinal direction labels to locate places on a simple map and apply the same orientation convention to a real space.
periods.section_context: Cardinal directions (North, South, East, West), compass rose, Navya's neighbourhood map, places in each direction from Navya's home.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'How does knowing which direction something is help you describe where it is to someone who has never been there?' This moves the skill from map-reading to practical communication.

periods.activity_title: My School's Compass: Placing Our School at the Centre
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students imagine their school at the centre and name buildings or areas in each direction (p. 28)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook neighbourhood map as reference; teacher's sketch of school-centred diagram on board

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple blank template on the board — a central box labelled 'Our School' with four arms pointing North, South, East, West. Teacher explains: just as Navya's map was centred on her home, today students will centre their map on their own school and fill in what lies in each direction. Students set up the same template in their notebooks.

Students work on the Write task from Textbook p. 28: they think about what they know lies north, south, east, and west of their school — a park, a bus stop, a market, a hospital — and write the name of each place (or 'open land', 'houses') in the correct arm of their template. Teacher prompts students who are unsure to think about which direction the morning sun comes from, and where the main road is.

Students share their entries in small groups. Teacher facilitates a brief class comparison: Do different students place the same feature in different directions? Why might that happen? (Different students may enter school from different gates or approach from different streets.) Teacher acknowledges that maps depend on who is drawing them and from where.

Students write one sentence describing where one landmark near their school is, using a cardinal direction: 'The ___ is to the ___ of our school.' Teacher asks several students to read their sentences aloud, building a shared verbal map of the school's surroundings.

periods.implied_lo: Students can place a known location at the centre of a simple spatial layout and correctly assign surrounding places to cardinal directions.
periods.section_context: School at centre, cardinal directions from school, neighbourhood landmarks (park, bus stop, market, hospital), spatial orientation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students disagree about which direction something lies, treat it as a productive puzzle: 'How could we check which of you is right?' — pointing toward the idea of using the sun's position or a compass.

periods.activity_title: Giving Directions: Landmarks, Turns, and the Way to Get There
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students give directions to a favourite place near school using landmarks and directional words (p. 29)

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the scenario from Textbook p. 29: imagine a new friend joins your class and wants to visit your favourite place near school — a park, a library, a small temple, a snack stall — but does not know the area at all. How would you describe the route? Teacher demonstrates one example set of directions from the school gate to an imaginary corner shop, using left, right, forward, and a landmark.

Students write their own set of directions in their notebooks, completing the task from Textbook p. 29. They choose their favourite place near school and write a step-by-step route description using directional words (left, right, forward, backward) and at least two landmarks. Teacher circulates and asks students to read their directions aloud to check for missing steps.

Students pair up: one partner reads their directions aloud while the other tries to follow the route mentally or trace it with a finger on an imaginary map. Listener gives feedback: 'I got confused at ___.' Partners swap and repeat. Teacher draws attention to what makes a direction clear — specific landmarks, named turns, distances given by landmarks rather than by time or number.

Whole-class share: two or three students read their directions and the class guesses which place they are heading to. Teacher highlights that clear directions serve the community — they help newcomers, visitors, and anyone who is lost. Brief reflection: When might you need to ask for — or give — directions in real life?

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct a clear set of route directions using directional vocabulary and landmarks that another person can follow.
periods.section_context: Route directions, left, right, forward, backward, landmarks (park, shop, hospital, bus stop), favourite place near school.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you ever had to give directions to someone older than you — a delivery person, a visitor? What words did you use?' This grounds the skill in real neighbourhood experience.

periods.activity_title: Drawing a Neighbourhood Map: Route from School to a Public Place
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students draw a map showing the route from their school to a public library or nearby public place, identifying landmarks (p. 30)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 30 sample map illustration as reference

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 30 and walks students through the map activity: they will draw a route map from their school to a nearby public place — a library, hospital, post office, or bus stop. Teacher reviews the conventions from earlier in the chapter: compass rose in one corner, simple symbols for landmarks, a short key if needed. Students gather their materials.

Students draw their route maps on paper or in their notebooks. They mark their school as the starting point, trace the route with a line, place at least three landmark symbols along the way (parks, shops, hospitals, bus stops), and add a compass rose. Teacher circulates, prompting: Have you shown which direction you travel? Have you labelled your landmarks? Is the start and end clearly marked?

Students share their maps with the person beside them, who traces the route with a finger and says one thing that is clear and one thing that could be made clearer. Students make one small revision based on the feedback. Teacher selects two or three maps that use landmarks in different ways and discusses what makes each effective.

Students write a one-sentence caption below their map: 'This map shows the route from ___ to ___ and uses landmarks like ___ to help a traveller find the way.' Maps are kept in notebooks for reference.

periods.implied_lo: Students can create a simple sketch map of a familiar route, using symbols, landmarks, and directional conventions to communicate spatial information.
periods.section_context: Route map from school to public place, landmarks (park, shop, hospital, bus stop), compass rose, symbols, map key.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to think about which landmarks are most useful — a large tree that might be cut down, or a building that has been there for many years? This surfaces the idea that stable landmarks make better map markers.

periods.activity_title: People and Vehicles of Community Services: Tabulating What We Know
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students list people involved and vehicles used in each community service (p. 32)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 32 table with example row

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 32 and introduces the tabulation task: students will list the people and vehicles involved in several neighbourhood community services. Teacher points to the example row already given in the textbook and asks students to read it. Students set up a matching table in their notebooks with columns for Service, People Involved, and Vehicles Used.

Students work individually or in pairs to fill the table for each community service shown — fire service, ambulance/health service, garbage collection, police, postal delivery. For each, they name at least one person (by role) and one vehicle. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck: 'When a fire engine arrives, who gets out? What is the driver's job called?'

Class builds a shared table on the board by calling on different pairs for each row. Teacher discusses any service where students gave different answers — for example, a health worker who travels by bicycle in a rural area versus by ambulance in a city — and notes that services may look different in different places.

Students write two sentences: 'The service that uses the most people is ___ because ___' and 'One service I had not thought about before was ___ because ___.' Teacher invites three or four students to share, celebrating observations that go beyond the obvious.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically record the human and material resources that make specific community services function.
periods.section_context: Fire service, ambulance, garbage collection, police service, postal delivery, roles (firefighter, nurse, sanitation worker, police officer, postman), vehicles (fire engine, ambulance, garbage truck, police van, postal van).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Are there people who keep our neighbourhood clean or safe who you have never really noticed before? Why might their work be invisible even though it is important?' This develops civic appreciation without directing students to a single answer.

periods.activity_title: Making Our Neighbourhood Better: Group Planning and Presentation
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Groups discuss what new services or facilities they would add to improve the neighbourhood and present how changes would help everyone (p. 31)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 31 and sets up the group task: each group of three or four students is in charge of making their neighbourhood better. They will decide on two or three new services or improvements, explain who would benefit and how, and then present their plan to the class.

Groups plan together on their large paper or notebook pages. They write or draw: (a) the service or facility they would add or improve, (b) who it would help, and (c) how it would make the neighbourhood better. Teacher circulates, asking: 'Is there anyone in the neighbourhood who is left out by the services that already exist? Who might need this most?'

Groups present their plans in turn — each group gets an unhurried but focused slot. Listening students may ask one question or suggest one addition. Teacher notes common themes (more green spaces, better health access, safer roads) on the board, building a shared picture of what a good neighbourhood looks like.

Teacher closes with a reflection: 'Every person in this room named something that would help someone else — that is what civic responsibility means.' Students write one sentence: 'One change that would help the most people in my neighbourhood is ___.' Notebooks are closed.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify a gap in community services and articulate a reasoned proposal for improvement that considers who benefits.
periods.section_context: Neighbourhood improvement, new services or facilities, community benefit, civic responsibility, group planning.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt groups to think about people who are sometimes overlooked — elderly residents, people with disabilities, very young children — to ensure their plans go beyond the obvious and reflect genuine civic thinking.

periods.activity_title: Exploring Our Neighbourhood: Connecting Everything We Have Learned
periods.textbook_anchor: Looking Around the Neighbourhood — Students discuss as a class the community helpers during COVID-19 and why thanking them matters (p. 31)
periods.visual_aids: Teacher's board summary diagram connecting the chapter's three strands: communication, banking/savings, neighbourhood infrastructure

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a simple web on the board with 'Our Neighbourhood' at the centre and three branches: 'How we communicate', 'How we save and use money', 'Public services around us'. Students call out what belongs on each branch — the teacher adds their contributions. This surfaces the full conceptual map of the chapter without requiring any specific earlier activity to have occurred.

Teacher opens Textbook p. 31 and reads the COVID-19 reflection task aloud: as a class, students recall — drawing on what elders around them have shared — who helped the community during that difficult time. Students name doctors, nurses, garbage collectors, shopkeepers, teachers, police, delivery workers. Teacher asks: What made each of these people important? Could the community have managed without any one of them?

Whole-class discussion: Which of the services and systems explored across this chapter — postal, banking, hospitals, transport, maps — would have mattered most in a moment of community crisis? Students reason aloud. Teacher draws connections between what students say and the chapter's two threads: the human-built systems (transport, communication, finance) and the civic responsibility and interdependence that keeps them running.

Students write a final reflection in their notebooks: 'My neighbourhood works because ___.' They complete the sentence in two or three sentences, naming at least two systems or services and the people who run them. Teacher invites three or four students to read their reflections. Teacher closes: every building, every service, every route on a map represents people choosing to build and maintain something for everyone — that is what a neighbourhood is.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect the functions of multiple community systems and explain how human interdependence keeps a neighbourhood working.
periods.section_context: Communication systems, banking and savings, public services (hospital, post office, police, library, fire service), community helpers during COVID-19, civic interdependence, neighbourhood as a shared system.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If one of these services disappeared tomorrow — the postal system, the hospital, the bank — what would change for your family and neighbours?' This synthesis question draws together every section's content through a single civic lens.

assessment_items.question_text: Navya drops a letter into the postbox on her way home. Before the letter reaches the person she wrote to, what does the postman do with it first?

options.label: A
options.text: Delivers it directly to the address written on the envelope

options.label: B
options.text: Takes it to the post office, where letters are sorted by region before being dispatched

options.label: C
options.text: Sends it by mobile phone to the nearest post office

options.label: D
options.text: Gives it to the bank so it can be delivered with money orders

assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option B. The sequence — postbox → postman collects → post office sorts by region → dispatch — is the key process this item checks.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a local community institution serves people by connecting them across distance.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not grasped the sorting and routing step — they think the postman acts as a direct courier, skipping the post office entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused modern digital communication with the physical postal process, merging two separate systems.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused two distinct institutions — the post office and the bank — that both appeared in the chapter's neighbourhood walk.

assessment_items.question_text: A student drew a timeline of how people have communicated across history. She placed 'mobile phones' before 'postal service'. Is her timeline correct? Explain why or why not, and write the correct order for these two methods.
expected_elements: States that the timeline is incorrect.
Identifies that the postal service came before mobile phones in the history of communication.
Places postal service earlier and mobile phones later in the correct sequence.
Gives a reason — such as mobile phones being a modern invention while postal services existed for much longer — to support the correction.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response corrects the error, states the right order, and gives at least one supporting reason. A response that only says 'incorrect' without ordering or reasoning earns partial credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can sequence a set of human-made systems in order of historical development and identify the direction of change.

assessment_items.question_text: Grandfather says: 'When I was your age, if I wanted to share news with a cousin in another city, I had to write a letter and wait many weeks for a reply.' Today, Navya can send a voice message and get a reply in seconds. Do you think faster communication has made life better in every way? Give reasons for and against, and share your own view.
look_for: Acknowledges at least one benefit of faster communication (e.g., news reaches people instantly, emergencies can be handled quickly).
Acknowledges at least one drawback or concern (e.g., wrong information spreads fast, people may send without thinking).
States a personal view and justifies it with reference to the chapter's content or their own experience.
Shows awareness that both slow and fast communication have served important purposes for people at different times.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response presents both sides and arrives at a reasoned personal position. A weak response lists only benefits or only drawbacks without weighing them.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare communication practices across generations and draw a reasoned conclusion about how changes in speed affect everyday life.

assessment_items.task: Write a short letter (five to eight sentences) to a real or imagined friend in another city. Your letter must include: your address at the top, a greeting, a short piece of news to share, a question for your friend, and a proper sign-off. When you are done, write the recipient's address and your return address on a separate slip as if it were the envelope.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My address: ___
Date: ___
Dear ___,
[Your news here — two or three sentences]
[Your question for your friend — one sentence]
Yours,
[Your name]

Envelope slip:
To: [Friend's name and address]
From: [Your name and address]
format_of_output: Handwritten letter with all five required parts
Separate address slip with recipient and sender addresses
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the student has included all five structural elements and addressed the envelope slip correctly. Content of the letter may vary freely — no fixed correct answer for the news or question.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can produce a structured written communication that follows a conventional format.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the conventional letter format — address, greeting, body, question, sign-off — and understands how the envelope connects to the postal system.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold breaks the letter into labelled parts so students know exactly what is expected in each section. The envelope slip checks whether students understand that the physical address is separate from the letter's body.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all five structural parts present, envelope slip correctly shows both addresses, body is coherent. Weak: missing the greeting or sign-off, no address on the slip, or body is a single disconnected sentence.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find sustained writing difficult may dictate their letter to the teacher, or complete the scaffold in bullet points before writing the final version.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The handwritten format directly enacts the chapter's activity task and makes the postal format tangible — the student produces an object that could actually be posted.

assessment_items.question_text: Navya's grandfather remembers going to the bank and standing in a long queue every time he needed cash. Navya can get cash any time, day or night, without queuing. Which invention makes this possible?
assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option C. The item specifically targets cash access at any hour without queuing — UPI transfers money but does not dispense cash, and the passbook and money order are record-keeping and transfer tools respectively.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare past and present methods of managing money and explain the role of a community financial institution.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses a record-keeping document with a cash-access technology — the passbook records transactions but cannot dispense money.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses a money-transfer tool (money order through the post office) with a cash-withdrawal machine — a category error between two different systems.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student knows UPI is a modern payment tool but has not distinguished between transferring money electronically and withdrawing physical cash at any time.

assessment_items.question_text: A Grade IV student looked at an Indian rupee note and said: 'It only shows one language because India has one official language.' Do you agree? What would you tell her after observing a currency note carefully?
expected_elements: States that the student's claim is incorrect.
Notes that an Indian currency note shows multiple languages (students should indicate the note carries more than one or two — the full panel has many regional languages).
Explains that this reflects India's linguistic diversity.
Mentions at least one other feature observed on the note (a symbol, a national emblem, the denomination, or a picture).
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response corrects the claim, names the linguistic diversity shown on the note, and adds at least one other observed feature. The exact number of languages named need not be precise — the key is that the student knows there are many.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured close observation of a familiar object and record specific details in an organised way.

assessment_items.question_text: Reema's family does not have a smartphone. She wants to send money to her grandmother who lives in another town. Which service could she use, and how does it work? Also name one other service — besides saving money — that a bank provides.
expected_elements: Names an appropriate money-transfer method for someone without a smartphone — such as a money order through the post office or a visit to the bank.
Briefly explains how that method works (e.g., money order: fill a form at the post office, pay the amount plus a fee, the post office delivers the money).
Names one additional bank service beyond savings (e.g., loans, fixed deposits, issuing a passbook, currency exchange).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any reasonable transfer method that does not require a smartphone. Accept any genuine additional bank service. The explanation of how the method works need only be two or three sentences.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the range of services provided by a local financial institution and explain the function of one specific technological tool within it.

assessment_items.task: You have been given ₹100 to use over one month. Make a budget plan showing how you will spend and save this money wisely. Your plan must include: at least three things you will spend money on (with amounts), how much you will save, and one sentence explaining what you are saving for.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My ₹100 Budget Plan

| Item | Amount (₹) | Why I chose this |
|---|---|---|
| ___ | ___ | ___ |
| ___ | ___ | ___ |
| ___ | ___ | ___ |

Total spent: ₹___
Amount saved: ₹___
I am saving because: ___
format_of_output: Completed budget table with at least three spending rows
One sentence giving a reason for saving
assessment_items.annotation: Check that the three amounts and the savings total add up to ₹100. The specific items chosen will vary — any reasonable spending categories are acceptable. The reason for saving should show forward thinking (future need, emergency, or goal).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can create a simple plan that balances spending and saving and explain the reasoning behind financial choices.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can distribute a fixed amount across spending and saving categories, check that totals balance, and articulate a purpose for saving.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table format guides students to name each item, assign an amount, and justify the choice. The saving row and reason sentence push beyond mere listing into purposeful planning.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: amounts add to exactly ₹100, at least three distinct categories, saving reason shows a specific future goal. Weak: amounts do not add to ₹100, only one or two items, saving reason is absent or vague ('for later').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the arithmetic difficult may use the scaffold column to tick the approximate amount and explain their choices verbally to the teacher.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Budget table with savings summary sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The table structure makes the arithmetic transparent and mirrors the real-world practice of planning expenditure — a life skill the chapter explicitly develops.

assessment_items.question_text: A health worker visits homes in a village every week to check on children's health and tell families about a health camp. Which type of community worker does this describe?

options.label: B
options.text: A community health visitor or ASHA worker

assessment_items.annotation: Accept option B. The item targets health outreach — a specific community health role introduced in the hospital sub-section. All distractors are genuine neighbourhood workers from the same chapter but serve different functions.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify people who work in local public institutions and explain how their roles serve the wider community.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student associates community safety with firefighters but has not linked the visiting and health-checking role to the health system specifically.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused the visiting-homes function with the postman's role — both visit homes, but for entirely different purposes.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has associated a neighbourhood worker with the general idea of community service but not with health outreach specifically.

assessment_items.question_text: Building a new flyover in a city makes travel faster and connects more areas. But Dada ji pointed out that building it required cutting many trees, and that birds and animals lost their homes. Do you think cities should keep building new transport infrastructure? What could be done to balance the benefits and the losses? Give reasons for your answer.
look_for: Acknowledges the benefit of new transport infrastructure — faster travel, better connectivity, more areas linked.
Acknowledges the environmental cost — trees cut, habitats lost for birds and animals.
Proposes at least one specific balancing action (e.g., planting trees elsewhere, building green bridges for animals, choosing routes that avoid forests).
Presents a reasoned personal position rather than simply describing both sides without taking a view.
Shows awareness that both human needs and environmental health matter — the trade-off is genuine, not one-sided.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response names both sides, proposes a concrete balancing measure, and expresses a reasoned view. A weak response only describes the benefit or only expresses concern without any proposed solution.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare past and present transportation practices, identifying both the benefits of new infrastructure and its environmental consequences.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at a simple map. The compass rose shows North at the top. The post office is drawn above the school, and the park is drawn to the right of the school. In which direction is the park from the school?
assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option C. With North at the top, right = East on a standard map. This item tests whether students have internalised the compass-rose convention, not just memorised where places appear on Navya's specific map.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use cardinal direction labels to locate places on a simple map and apply the same orientation convention to a real space.

competency.competency_text: Draws a sketch of their school, village, and ward using symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused 'right on the page' with 'up on the page' — they are reading position as North rather than using the compass rose convention.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be applying a reversal rule incorrectly, associating 'right' with South rather than East.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused East and West — a common direction-pair error where students know the convention involves left and right but swap which side is which.

assessment_items.question_text: Imagine your school is at the centre of a map. Name one place you would find to the North of your school and one place to the South. Then explain how knowing the direction of a place helps you describe where it is to someone who has never visited.
expected_elements: Names a specific place (building, landmark, or area) to the North of their school.
Names a specific place to the South of their school.
Explains — in one or two sentences — why knowing a direction makes it easier to describe a location to someone unfamiliar with the area.
assessment_items.annotation: The specific landmarks named will vary by school location — accept any reasonable and plausible answer. Award full marks if the direction-explanation shows that the student understands directions as a shared reference system, not just a personal view of left and right.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can place a known location at the centre of a simple spatial layout and correctly assign surrounding places to cardinal directions.

Explains — in one or two sentences — why knowing a direction makes it easier to describe a location to someone unfamiliar with the area.

assessment_items.question_text: A new student joins your class and wants to find the nearest bus stop from school. Write step-by-step directions from the school gate to the bus stop, using at least two landmarks and directional words (left, right, forward).
expected_elements: Begins directions from the school gate.
Uses directional words — left, right, forward — at least twice.
Names at least two landmarks along the route.
Ends with a clear indication that the traveller has arrived at the bus stop.
assessment_items.annotation: Specific routes and landmarks will vary by school location — accept any response that follows a logical sequence, uses directional words, and names at least two real or plausible landmarks. Assess the structure of the directions, not the specific geography.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a clear set of route directions using directional vocabulary and landmarks that another person can follow.

expected_elements: Begins directions from the school gate.
Uses directional words — left, right, forward — at least twice.
Names at least two landmarks along the route.

assessment_items.task: Draw a map showing the route from your school to the nearest public place (library, hospital, park, post office, or bus station). On your map: mark your school as the starting point, draw the route as a line, place symbols for at least three landmarks along the way, add a compass rose showing North, and write a short key explaining what your symbols mean.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Steps to follow:
1. Draw your school and label it 'Start'.
2. Draw the route as a line from school to the public place.
3. Draw symbols for at least three landmarks (e.g., a tree for a park, a cross for a hospital).
4. Draw a compass rose in one corner.
5. Write a key: Symbol → What it means.
6. Label the public place at the end of your route.
format_of_output: At least three labelled landmark symbols
assessment_items.annotation: The specific route and landmarks will vary by school location — accept any map that includes all five required elements. Assess the completeness of the map's conventions (compass rose, key, labelled start and end), not the accuracy of distances.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can create a simple sketch map of a familiar route, using symbols, landmarks, and directional conventions to communicate spatial information.

competency.competency_text: Draws a sketch of their school, village, and ward using symbols and directions

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate spatial knowledge of their neighbourhood into a conventional map format with symbols, a compass rose, and a key.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The six-step scaffold breaks map-making into a manageable sequence. Each step adds one map element — students who follow all six will have produced a complete map.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all five required elements present, symbols are consistent with the key, compass rose correctly positioned, route is traceable from start to end. Weak: missing compass rose or key, landmarks drawn but not labelled, start and end not marked.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students with fine-motor difficulties may draw larger, simpler symbols and use a ruler for the route line. Students may verbally describe the route while a peer draws it, as a collaborative alternative.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The hand-drawn format directly practises the chapter's map-drawing skill and produces a spatial product the teacher can assess against the five required conventions.

assessment_items.question_text:
Complete the table below for two community services.

| Service | One person who works there (and their role) | One vehicle used |
|---|---|---|
| Fire service | | |
| Garbage collection | | |

Then write one sentence: which of these services do you think is most often overlooked by people, and why?
expected_elements: Names a correct worker and role for the fire service (e.g., firefighter — fights fires and rescues people).
Names a correct vehicle for the fire service (e.g., fire engine).
Names a correct worker and role for garbage collection (e.g., sanitation worker — collects and removes waste to keep the neighbourhood clean).
Names a correct vehicle for garbage collection (e.g., garbage truck).

Writes a sentence identifying one of the two services as often overlooked and gives a reason (e.g., sanitation workers are overlooked because their work happens early in the morning before most people are awake).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any correct worker-role and vehicle pairing for each service. The 'overlooked' sentence is evaluative — accept any reasoned response that names a service and gives a plausible reason for its invisibility.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically record the human and material resources that make specific community services function.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

assessment_items.task: Your group has been given the task of improving your neighbourhood. Choose one new service or facility you would add (or one existing one you would improve). Draw or write a plan showing: what the service is, who it would help most, and how it would make the neighbourhood better. Be ready to explain your plan in two or three sentences.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Our neighbourhood improvement plan:

Service or facility we would add/improve: ___

Who it would help most: ___

How it would make the neighbourhood better: ___

[Draw or write your plan here]
format_of_output: Two-to-three sentence spoken or written explanation
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any realistic neighbourhood service or facility. Assess whether the student has identified a specific group who benefits (not just 'everyone') and whether their explanation connects the service to a real community need.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify a gap in community services and articulate a reasoned proposal for improvement that considers who benefits.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can move from observing what exists in a neighbourhood to proposing a reasoned improvement grounded in community need — a civic planning skill.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-part scaffold separates what (the service), who (the beneficiary), and how (the improvement mechanism). Students who address all three parts have produced a complete proposal.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: service is specific (not just 'a park'), beneficiary group is named precisely (e.g., elderly residents, young children), explanation shows a clear link between the service and a real gap. Weak: very generic service, 'everyone' as beneficiary without specificity, explanation restates the service without explaining the benefit.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may draw their plan rather than write it, or present verbally to the teacher. Groups may produce a single shared plan rather than individual ones.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written or drawn neighbourhood improvement plan with brief explanation
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The open format matches the group discussion task from the chapter and gives students who express themselves better through drawing equal access to demonstrating the skill.

assessment_items.question_text: During COVID-19, many people worked hard to keep neighbourhoods safe and running — doctors, nurses, garbage collectors, shopkeepers, teachers, delivery workers, and others. Choose two of these community workers. For each, explain: (a) what service they provided, and (b) how the neighbourhood would have been different without them. Then write one sentence about what you think makes a community strong.
look_for: Names two specific community workers from the chapter (or reasonable equivalents).
Explains what each worker did — their service — in concrete terms.
For each worker, describes how the neighbourhood would have been different or worse without them — shows genuine consequence reasoning.
Writes a concluding sentence that captures a general principle about community strength (e.g., communities are strong when people depend on and help each other).
Draws on content from across the chapter — communication, public services, civic responsibility — rather than only the COVID-19 prompt.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response names two workers, explains their role concretely, reasons about the absence of each, and produces a general principle. A weak response lists workers without explaining consequences or produces a concluding sentence that merely restates the prompt.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect the functions of multiple community systems and explain how human interdependence keeps a neighbourhood working.
